To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the binding of the drug WIN51711 in the Sabin strain type 3 polio virus induces only small changes in the structure, while the same drug induces large conformational rearrangements in human rhinoverus 14.
the binding of the antivirial drug WIN51711 does not induce significant structural changes in poliovirus, unlike the binding of the same drug to rhinoviruses.

the drug WIN51711 binds to the sabin poliovirus in a pocket formed by residues in the capsid protein VP-1, and that binding to poliovirus has a much greater stabilizing effect on the virus than does binding to the closely related rhinovirus HRV 14.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of the poliovirus capsid protein, and how it interacts with the viral RNA and other molecules.
the structure, assembly and stability of viral capsids.

understanding the structural and functional basis of the antivirals, which are used for the treatment of viral infections, and to develop new drugs to fight against viruses, which cause serious diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WIN51711 binds in an extended conformation, in the same pocket, and in the same orientation in both viruses, but the effect of the drug binding is different.
WIN51711 is a potent inhibitor of poliovirus uncoating and that the binding of this inhibitor in P3/Sabine does not induce significant structural changes in the coat protein.
the drug WIN51711 binds to the sabin type 3 polio virus in the same manner as it does in rhinoviruses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have solved the structure of poliovirus complexed with an inhibitor that is a lead compound in the search for a drug against polio.

the drug binding in the P3/Sabin virus is not accompanied by large conformational change in the structure of VP1, while the drug binding in rhino-virus induces significant changes in the VP1 structure.
the structure of the drug in the poliovirus capsid is similar to the structure observed in rhinoviruses.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the structure of the drug binding site in the capsid protein is not conserved among the two different viruses, and that the drug binds to the site in a different orientation in the two viruses, despite the high level of sequence identity between the capsids of these viruses.
, in poliovirus, the drug binding site is a blind pocket, whereas in HRV14 it is a cleft, so that the drug is more exposed to the solvent.
, in the case of poliovirus, the binding of WIN to the virus capsid induces very few structural changes in the protein.
